mcqs.question: A single database row typically sustains a few thousand increments/sec before lock contention dominates. What does this mean for a viral video generating ~2,800 views/sec?
options: Nothing — 2,800/sec is comfortably within a single row's capacity with room to spare
The row's ceiling is a hardware limit that can be fixed by using a faster disk
A single hot row's write ceiling is close to or below what one popular object alone can generate, before counting any other objects
This is only a problem if the video also has more than 1M views total
mcqs.explanation: A single row's lock-contention ceiling can be at or near what one viral object alone demands, with no room for other simultaneously popular objects — that gap is exactly why this needs a distributed design. It isn't a disk-speed issue, it's about lock contention; and total view count doesn't matter as much as the sustained rate.

mcqs.question: In-memory batching before flushing to durable storage cuts write volume dramatically. What's the explicit cost of this approach?
options: It requires a distributed transaction on every increment
It makes reads slower than a single-row counter
It cannot be combined with sharding
A small window of increments can be lost if a server crashes before flushing its in-memory batch
mcqs.explanation: Batching trades a small, bounded risk of losing unflushed increments on a crash for a large reduction in write volume — an explicit trade-off tied to whether the counter needs to be exact. It doesn't require distributed transactions, doesn't inherently slow reads, and combines naturally with sharding.

mcqs.question: Why would an ad-billing system likely prefer a strongly consistent single-row counter over a sharded, batched one, despite the throughput cost?
options: Single-row counters are always faster than sharded counters
Billing needs an exact count, and a batched sharded counter can lose or lag increments in a way that's unacceptable when money is involved
Sharded counters cannot technically support a getCount operation
Billing systems are legally required to avoid sharding
mcqs.explanation: The deciding factor is the exactness requirement: billing needs every increment accounted for precisely, and batching's small loss window is unacceptable there, even though it costs raw throughput. Single-row counters are typically slower under load, not faster; sharded counters do support getCount; there's no such legal rule.

mcqs.question: Why is HyperLogLog a fundamentally different tool than a sharded increment counter, even though both are used for "counting"?
options: HyperLogLog is just a faster implementation of the same sharded-counter idea
HyperLogLog only works for counts under 1,000
HyperLogLog estimates distinct/unique counts using fixed small memory, solving a problem a plain event counter can't handle without tracking every individual ID
HyperLogLog requires exact consistency, unlike sharded counters
mcqs.explanation: A plain sharded counter counts total events cheaply but can't dedupe repeated events from the same source; HyperLogLog specifically estimates distinct cardinality in fixed memory, which is a different problem. It isn't just a faster version of sharding, isn't limited to small counts, and is itself approximate, not exact.

mcqs.question: A popular video's view count is summed live across all shards on every single page load. What's the actual problem with this?
options: It multiplies read load by the shard count, turning a cheap display value into an expensive query that can dwarf the original write-side problem
It causes the write-side shards to become inconsistent with each other
It is impossible to implement correctly with more than 2 shards
It only affects counters that use HyperLogLog
mcqs.explanation: Reading the sum on every request multiplies per-read cost by the number of shards — for a counter read far more often than it's written, this can create a bigger bottleneck than the one sharding was meant to fix; caching the total avoids it. It doesn't cause write-side inconsistency, works fine at any shard count, and has nothing to do with HyperLogLog specifically.
